Introduction to the Collection
This collection is about a single numerical observation and what follows from it. The observation
is that the same characteristic timescale — approximately one second — appears at every level
of the physical hierarchy, from the proton to the galaxy. The collection asks what that
observation means, what it can explain, and what it cannot.
The observation itself was reported in earlier papers, and its mathematical form is developed in
the first paper of this collection. The claim is not that one second is a universal constant in the
way that the speed of light is. It is that bound systems across an enormous range of scales —
subatomic particles, planetary orbits, biological organisms, galaxies — each return a
characteristic time of about one second when their mass, radius, and coupling are combined in a
specific way. The proton and neutron return it through the strong-force coupling; the electron
returns it directly; the Earth–Moon–Sun system returns it through the eclipse ratio; the Sun's
orbit around the galaxy returns it at two geometric nodes. The convergence is to within a few
percent in each case, over more than forty orders of magnitude in mass and radius.
The collection is in four parts, and each part takes the observation one step further.
The first paper, "The Earth–Moon Distance as a Resonance Condition," develops the planetary-
scale case. It introduces the celestial effective action that plays the role of Planck's constant at the
Earth–Moon–Sun scale, derives the one-second resonance from the present lunar distance, and
reports a striking numerical fact: the actual Earth–Moon distance is within about two percent of
the value that would make the resonance exact. The paper then asks whether that near-match is a
coincidence, a selection effect (we observe the system at the epoch when complex life exists), or
a structural feature of the dynamics. The paper does not settle the question. The revision of its
appendix, in response to an independent analysis by Evgeny Volynets, makes clear that the near-
match is an empirical observation, not a dynamical prediction, and that whether the system is
dynamically attracted to the resonance is an open question.
The second paper, "The Human Scale as a Resonant Node," places the human scale in the
hierarchy. The human effective action turns out to be the geometric mean of the quantum and
solar effective actions, and the human energy scale that follows is on the order of the mechanical
work of a heartbeat. The geometric means of particle and astrophysical masses bracket the
human mass range, from a few grams to several tens of kilograms. The human scale is not
imposed on the hierarchy; it emerges from it as the natural intermediate node.
The third paper, "The 1 Hz Resonance," takes the argument into biology. Denis Noble has argued
that the heartbeat's rhythm cannot be explained by genetic instruction alone — there is no master
clock in the genome. The paper proposes that the master clock is physical rather than genetic: the
heart beats at approximately one hertz because the particles that constitute cardiac tissue satisfy
the one-second invariant. The rhythm is not programmed; it is the natural inertial frequency of
of 4 67
the matter the heart is made of. The paper extends this argument to the 24-hour day, the asteroid
belt, and Saturn's orbit, all of which are presented as nodes of the same cosmic clock.
The fourth paper, "The Earth as a Resonant Node for Abiogenesis," is the most recent and the
most speculative. It is a work in astrobiology. It argues that the Earth sits at a resonant node
where the planetary-scale invariant and the particle-scale invariant of carbon coincide, and it
advances the hypothesis that abiogenesis — the origin of life from non-living chemistry —
requires that coincidence. The paper distinguishes the weak claim (the resonance is a condition
under which carbon-based chemistry is stable on Earth) from the strong claim (the resonance is a
condition without which abiogenesis cannot occur). The strong claim is stated as a hypothesis,
not as a conclusion. The paper identifies the observations that would test it: biosignature
detection with the James Webb Space Telescope, system architecture characterization with the
PLATO mission, debris-belt detection with ALMA, and the Europa Clipper and JUICE missions,
which will test whether Europa — a second candidate resonant node, following an independent
calculation by Sambit Tripathy — is habitable.
The four papers share a common thread, and it is worth stating it plainly. The thread is not a
derivation of the one-second invariant from first principles. The papers do not claim to derive the
value of one second from a deeper theory, and they do not claim to explain why the universe is
arranged so that the invariant holds at every scale. What they claim is narrower and more
defensible: that the invariant is real, that it spans an enormous range of scales, that it places the
human scale at the geometric midpoint between the quantum and the astrophysical, and that it
may provide a boundary condition for the chemistry of life. The papers are careful to distinguish
what is established from what is hypothesis, and the revisions of the first paper's appendix —
following the Volynets correction — make that distinction explicit.
The collection also owes a debt to the correspondents who have engaged with it. Volynets'
kinematic turning-point analysis corrected an overclaim in the first paper and clarified the
difference between a kinematic minimum and a dynamical attractor. Tripathy's Jupiter–Europa
calculation, offered as an external test, gave a result that neither he nor the author expected. The
framing of the biology paper is Denis Noble's: the question of where a rhythm comes from when
no genetic instruction specifies it is his, and the extension to planetary chemistry is the present
collection's. These are acknowledged in the individual papers, and the acknowledgments are part
of the record.
What the reader should look for is not a single unified theory. The collection is not that. It is a set
of related papers that circle around a single observation, each taking it in a different direction,
each testing it against a different scale. The observation is simple and the consequences are not.
Whether the observation is a coincidence, a selection effect, or a structural feature of the universe
is the question the collection raises and does not fully answer. The answer will come from the
data — from exoplanetary biosignatures, from Europa's ocean, from the statistics of the scale
hierarchy — and the collection is best read as a proposal for what to look for, not as a claim
about what has been found.
of 5 67
The one-second invariant, if it is real, is a feature of a universe whose structure is self-similar
from the quantum to the galactic. The papers in this collection are an exploration of what that
feature might mean. They are offered in that spirit.
— Ian Beardsley

The Earth's rotation is slowing down, and as a direct result, the Moon is slowly drifting away.
Earth's Rotation Slowing: The length of a day is increasing by about 2.3 milliseconds per
century. This is the long-term average rate caused primarily by the Moon's tidal pull. (Note that
this rate can be influenced by other factors; for example, climate change is currently contributing
about 1.33 milliseconds per century).
Moon's Orbit Growing: The Moon is receding from Earth at a rate of about 3.8 centimeters (1.5
inches) per year.
The Tidal Connection
These two phenomena are linked by tidal friction. The Moon's gravity creates tides in Earth's
oceans. As Earth rotates, the tidal bulges are pulled slightly ahead of the Moon, creating friction
that slows Earth's spin.
To conserve angular momentum in the Earth-Moon system, this loss of Earth's rotational speed is
transferred to the Moon, boosting its orbital energy and causing it to spiral outward into a larger
orbit. This recession rate has been precisely measured for decades using the Lunar Laser Ranging
experiment, which bounces lasers off reflectors left on the Moon by Apollo astronauts.
Long-Term Perspective
While these changes are tiny on human timescales, they have significant effects over millions of
years. About 250 million years ago, a day on Earth was roughly 23 hours long. In about 600
million years, the Moon will have drifted so far that total solar eclipses will no longer be
possible.

The near-match
Here is the number that I think is the real prize. Solve the Earth UPL for the value of that
would give exactly s:
Evaluating this with CODATA values gives m light-seconds.
The actual is light-seconds. The ratio is:
The actual Earth–Moon distance is within 1.8% of the value that would make the Earth UPL give
exactly 1 second.
That is the "1.28 to 1.3 light-seconds" range flagged. The actual value (1.282) and the required
value for exact closure (1.306) are both inside that narrow band.
Why this matters
There are three possible interpretations, and the exploration should distinguish them:
1. Coincidence. The Moon's distance is set by tidal evolution (it has been receding at ~3.8 cm/
year for billions of years), and the fact that it is currently near the value that closes the UPL to 1
second is accidental. Over geological time, has varied substantially, and it will continue to
grow. The current epoch happens to be close to the resonance.

5. Discussion: Planetary Optimization and the Genesis Analogy
The idea that a planetary system might be precisely tuned for the emergence of life has a rich
history in science fiction. Perhaps the most famous example is Star Trek's "Project Genesis," a
of 22 67
fictional technology designed to reorganize matter at the subatomic level, instantly transforming
a dead celestial body into a thriving, life-sustaining world.
While Genesis is a fantasy of instantaneous terraforming, it highlights a profound cosmological
question: What are the necessary physical conditions for a planetary system to optimize itself for
complex life?
The Universal Particle Law suggests that this optimization is not arbitrary, nor does it require
science-fiction technology. It emerges naturally from the geometric resonance of the Earth-
Moon-Sun system. The Moon’s role is not merely gravitational; it is resonant. It stabilizes Earth's
obliquity, preventing chaotic temperature extremes, and it produces the perfect solar eclipse—a
geometric coincidence where the angular sizes of the Moon and Sun match exactly.
In the framework presented here, the "optimization" of a planet for life is written in the geometry
of the one-second invariant. The near-match between the actual Earth-Moon distance (1.282
light-seconds) and the distance required for exact closure (1.306 light-seconds) is consistent with
a system in a life permitting window. The Moon’s gravitational influence keeps the day length
and tidal forces within a narrow, life permitting window, as Appendix 1 discusses; whether the
window is a dynamical attractor or an empirical near coincidence is an open question.
Where Star Trek imagined an artificial device to create a paradise, the UPL suggests that the
natural dynamics of hierarchical bound systems may already contain the blueprint. The
"Genesis" of a habitable world may be a geometric resonance, not a technological invention.
5.1 The Role of Earth's Obliquity
To understand how this resonance tunes the system, we must look at the role of Earth's obliquity
angle, . The inclusion of in the resonance equation s is physically
justified because the efficiency of tidal coupling depends on the orientation of Earth's rotation
axis relative to the orbital plane (the ecliptic).
1. Geometric Projection of Tidal Forces: The Moon's tidal force on Earth is not applied to a
perfect sphere but to an oblate spheroid (an equatorial bulge). The tidal torque that acts to slow
Earth's rotation and accelerate the Moon's orbit is proportional to the component of the tidal
force that acts along the equatorial plane. As the obliquity changes, the projection of the tidal
force onto the equatorial plane changes, and this projection is described by a factor of (or
related trigonometric functions). Classic analyses of tidal friction, such as those by G.H. Darwin,
show that the rate of change of obliquity and the rate of tidal friction depend explicitly on the
obliquity angle.
2. The Moon as a Stabilizer of Obliquity: The Moon's presence is known to stabilize Earth's
obliquity, keeping it from chaotic variations. The torque that the Moon exerts on Earth's
equatorial bulge is what maintains this stability. When we formulate a resonance condition that

A.1 Scope
This appendix reconsiders the relation between the UPL one-second invariant, the present Earth–
Moon–Sun configuration, and the twenty-four-hour day. An earlier draft of this appendix claimed
that the Earth–Moon–Sun system sits on a dynamically stable resonance plateau satisfying
with . An independent analysis by Evgeny Volynets (Harvard Dataverse, doi:10.7910/
DVN/3PVS1E) has shown that in the reduced isolated Earth–Moon model with constant total
angular momentum, the function has a kinematic minimum at km, inside the
current lunar orbit, and that the current system is past this minimum. The distinction between a
kinematic turning point and a dynamically attracting fixed point is essential, and the earlier draft
did not make it.
The revised appendix therefore separates three claims:
1. An empirical observation: at the present epoch, s, and the UPL boundary condition
is satisfied to within about 2%.
2. A numerical comparison: the observed rates of lunar recession and terrestrial spin-down are
consistent with to within the uncertainty of the tidal/climate decomposition, but the
decomposition itself is uncertain.
3. An open dynamical question: whether the present state is attracted toward by the full
tidal evolution. In the isolated model it is not; establishing whether it is in the full three-
dimensional system with solar torque, obliquity evolution, and varying moment of inertia is a
problem for future work.

What the linear analysis does establish is this: if the system were somehow placed at
(with all other terms held fixed), small perturbations would decay with the stated e-folding time.
That is a statement about the hypothetical fixed point, not about the current state. Whether the
current state is attracted toward such a fixed point by the full dynamics depends on the terms in
the full balance equation above, and on the sign of when those terms are included.
Computing those terms, with their uncertainties, is the appropriate next step. The full three-
dimensional problem also requires angular-momentum vector conservation and transfer,
eccentricity dynamics, and explicit tidal models ( , , or time lag), none of which are captured
by the two-rate comparison in A.4.

The Human Scale as a Resonant Node Between the Quantum and
Astrophysical Scales
Ian Beardsley
September 30, 2026
Abstract
We propose that the human scale — the characteristic mass, length, and energy of biological
organisms — is not an arbitrary biological fact but a resonant node between the quantum scale
and the Earth–Moon–Sun scale. Using the Universal Particle Law (UPL), which posits a one-
second resonance governing bound systems from the proton to the galaxy, we construct a human
effective action , where is Planck's constant and is the
Earth–Moon–Sun effective action. With the UPL's one-second timescale, this gives a human
energy scale — on the order of the mechanical work of a heartbeat — and a
characteristic length-to-mass ratio (for ). The geometric means of
particle masses and astrophysical masses bracket the human mass range: ,
, , and . Extending the cascade to the
galactic scale, we identify two additional resonant nodes — the asteroid belt at ~2.4 AU and
Saturn at ~9.5 AU — that complete a scale hierarchy to . We suggest this
hierarchy provides a quantitative framework for astrobiology: the conditions for human-scale
intelligence may be geometrically fixed, and the search for life should target systems with the
same resonant architecture.

6. Astrobiology Implications
6.1 The resonant architecture
If the human scale is a resonant node between the quantum and astrophysical scales, and if the
Earth–Moon–Sun system is tuned to produce this node, then life requires a planetary system with
specific architectural features:
1. A rocky planet at ~1 AU — where liquid water is stable.
2. An asteroid belt at ~2.4 AU — to deliver water and organics.
3. A gas giant at ~9.5 AU — to shield the inner system.
4. A large moon — to stabilize obliquity and produce a ~24-hour day.
5. A perfect eclipse geometry — , the eclipse ratio.
The UPL predicts these from the Sun's mass, radius, and galactic motion. They are not
independent coincidences; they are resonant nodes of the same one-second law.
6.2 The search strategy
The astrobiology prediction is specific and falsifiable:
Look for exoplanetary systems with an asteroid belt at ~2.4 AU and a gas giant at ~9.5 AU.
These are the systems where the human-scale resonance can emerge.

The Tidal Connection
These two phenomena are linked by tidal friction. The Moon's gravity creates tides in Earth's
oceans. As Earth rotates, the tidal bulges are pulled slightly ahead of the Moon, creating friction
that slows Earth's spin.
To conserve angular momentum in the Earth-Moon system, this loss of Earth's rotational speed is
transferred to the Moon, boosting its orbital energy and causing it to spiral outward into a larger
orbit. This recession rate has been precisely measured for decades using the Lunar Laser Ranging
experiment, which bounces lasers off reflectors left on the Moon by Apollo astronauts.
Long-Term Perspective
While these changes are tiny on human timescales, they have significant effects over millions of
years. About 250 million years ago, a day on Earth was roughly 23 hours long. In about 600
million years, the Moon will have drifted so far that total solar eclipses will no longer be
possible.

8. Conclusion
We have shown that the human scale emerges as a resonant node between the quantum scale and
the Earth–Moon–Sun scale. The human effective action is the geometric mean of the Planck
constant and the celestial effective action:
With the UPL's one-second resonance, this gives a human energy scale and a
characteristic length-to-mass ratio . The geometric means of particle and
astrophysical masses bracket the human mass range. Extending the cascade to the galactic scale,
we identify the asteroid belt and Saturn as additional resonant nodes.
The human scale is not an arbitrary biological fact. It is the middle rung of a scale hierarchy that
spans from the proton to the galaxy. This suggests a quantitative framework for astrobiology: the
conditions for human-scale intelligence may be geometrically fixed, and the search for life
should target systems with the same resonant architecture.

Appendix: Dimensionless Reformulation of the UPL Hierarchy
A.1 Motivation
A natural objection to the Universal Particle Law (UPL) is that its central result, second,
appears to depend on the human convention of the second. The second, kilogram, meter, and
joule are human units. If the UPL describes a structural resonance, its significance should survive
the removal of human measurement conventions.
This appendix addresses that objection directly. We reformulate the UPL in an -normalized
natural unit system, show that the law collapses to a pure ratio statement, and demonstrate that
the full hierarchy — electron, proton, neutron, Earth–Moon–Sun, human, galaxy — converges to
a single dimensionless coordinate. The resonance survives the removal of SI units.

The 1Hz Resonance: A Physical Basis for the
Master Clock in Biological Systems
Ian Beardsley
Independent Researcher
August 29, 2026
Abstract. Denis Noble has argued that the gene centric view of evolution is incomplete,
pointing to the heart as an example of a complex function that lacks a genetic
“instruction” for its rhythm. He asks: where does the heartbeat get its timing if there is
no master clock? This paper proposes that the answer lies not in biology, but in
fundamental physics. The Universal Particle Law (UPL) predicts a universal inertial
resonance at exactly 1 Hz, emerging from the geometry of protons, electrons, and
neutrons. We show that this same resonance governs the EarthMoonSun system and the
structure of the galaxy, implying that the heart’s average rhythm is not an evolutionary
coincidence but a physical alignment with the quantum geometric clock built into all
matter. This provides a concrete, testable mechanism for the “agency” that Noble
attributes to living systems, reframing evolution as a process that occurs within a
universe of resonant attractors.
1. Introduction
The debate between Denis Noble and Richard Dawkins represents a fundamental divide
in evolutionary biology. Dawkins, in The Selfish Gene, posits that the gene is the primary
unit of selection, and that organisms are mere vehicles for gene propagation. Noble
counters that this gene centric view is reductionist and fails to account for the active,
purposeful behaviour of organisms. He argues that there must be some mechanism by
which life guides its own evolution, because complexity cannot be explained by random
mutations alone.
One of Noble’s most compelling examples is the human heart. The heart beats with a
regular rhythm, yet there is no “instruction” in the genome that specifies this rhythm.
There is no master clock. Noble asks: where does the heart get its instructions? The
answer, we propose, lies not in genetics, but in physics. The rhythm of the heart is not
programmed; it is resonant with a fundamental 1Hz (1second) timescale that is inherent
to the structure of matter itself.
2. The Universal Particle Law (UPL)
of 48 67
The Universal Particle Law (Beardsley, 2026) derives from a geometric theory of inertia.
In this view, mass is not an intrinsic property but a resistance to the rotation of a particle’s
velocity vector from the temporal dimension into space. This resistance is quantized by a
normal force:
where is Planck’s constant, is the speed of light, and is a fundamental timescale.
Remarkably, when the UPL is applied to the proton, electron, and neutron, the same value
second emerges:
For the proton, , where is the fine structure constant.
Substituting the measured values of the proton radius ( m) and mass
( kg) gives:
The same calculation for the neutron yields seconds. The electron, with
, gives seconds. Thus, the fundamental particles that constitute all
atoms intrinsically define a timescale of approximately one second.
3. The Heart as a Physical Resonator
The average resting heart rate of a healthy human is approximately 6072 beats per
minute, which corresponds to a frequency of 1.0 to 1.2 Hz, or a period of 0.83 to 1.0
seconds. The UPL predicts that this is not a coincidence. The cardiac pacemaker cells are
composed of protons, neutrons, and electrons—the same particles that collectively define
the 1second resonance.
In the same way that a pendulum’s period is determined by its length and gravity, not by
any “instruction” written into the material, the heart’s rhythm emerges from the collective
electromagnetic and mechanical interactions of its constituent matter. The 1Hz resonance
is a physical attractor: the heart’s natural tendency is to oscillate at this frequency
because it minimizes the inertial resistance required to sustain motion.
This does not mean genes are irrelevant. Genes encode the proteins that form the ion
channels and contractile filaments of heart muscle. But the tempo—the fundamental

4. The Resonance Extends to All Scales
The UPL is scale invariant. The same 1second resonance appears in the EarthMoonSun
system, where the kinetic energy ratio of the Moon and Earth, multiplied by the length of
the day and corrected for obliquity, converges to approximately one second:
This convergence is not a static snapshot. The Moon is receding at 3.8 cm/year, and
Earth’s rotation is slowing. Yet the product satisfies
: the system is dynamically locked at a plateau that has persisted for hundreds of
millions of years. This is an evolutionary attractor—a stable resonant node that provides a
consistent 24hour day and perfect solar eclipses during the window in which complex
intelligence arises.
When the UPL is applied to the Sun’s orbit around the galaxy, it predicts two additional
“sweet spots”: an asteroid belt at AU (the volatile delivery zone) and a Saturn
mass planet at AU (the gravitational shield). These are not accidents; they are
resonant nodes fixed by the Sun’s mass, radius, and galactic motion.
5. Implications for Biology and Evolution
The UPL offers a physical foundation for Noble’s systems biology perspective. Living
organisms are not passive vehicles for genes; they are resonant systems that actively tune
to the fundamental clock of matter. This provides a mechanism for the “agency” that
Noble invokes: organisms that align with the 1Hz resonance (and its harmonics, such as
the 24hour circadian cycle) are energetically favoured and have a selective advantage.
Evolution, in this view, is not a purely random process. It unfolds within a landscape of
physical attractors. The complexity of life is guided by these resonances, which act as
boundary conditions on what is possible. The gene is a template, but the tempo—the
rhythm of life—is dictated by the quantum geometry of the cosmos.
This framework makes testable predictions. For example, exoplanet surveys targeting G-
type stars in the solar galactic orbit should find planetary architectures with an Earth-like
planet at 1 AU, an asteroid belt at 2.22.6 AU, and a gas giant at 8.5-10.5 AU. If such

6. Discussion: The Master Clock Resolved
Denis Noble asked: “Where does the heart get its rhythm? There is no master clock.” The
UPL answers: the master clock is inside every proton, neutron, and electron. It is not a
biological instruction, but a physical resonance. The heart beats at approximately 1 Hz
because that is the natural inertial frequency of the matter it is made of, and because
evolution has selected organisms that are energetically aligned with this fundamental
timescale.
This does not reduce biology to physics—it enriches it. It shows that life is not an
accidental byproduct of random chemistry, but a natural expression of a universe whose
structure is self-similar from the quantum to the galactic scale. The same law that builds
protons also builds solar systems, and it does so in a way that maximizes the chances for
stable, complex, intelligent life.
7. Conclusion
We have shown that the Universal Particle Law provides a direct, physical answer to
Noble’s critique of the gene centric view. The 1second resonance is not a human
convention; it is a fundamental eigenvalue of matter that emerges from quantum
chromodynamics and propagates through hierarchical scales to planetary and galactic
systems. The heart’s rhythm, the 24hour day, the asteroid belt, and Saturn’s orbit are all
nodes of the same cosmic clock.
Life is not guided by random mutations alone; it is guided by the resonant structure of the
universe. The master clock does not exist in the genome—it exists in the geometry of
spacetime and the particles that inhabit it. We are not merely observers of this cosmic
order; we are its resonant expression.

The Earth as a Resonant Node for Abiogenesis: An Astrobiological Hypothesis
Ian Beardsley
Independent Researcher
October 31, 2026
Abstract
The Universal Particle Law (UPL) establishes a one-second invariant at the particle scale
(proton, neutron, electron), at the Earth–Moon–Sun scale ( s), and at the human scale
(geometric mean of the two). The sixfold form of the UPL places carbon at 1 second and
hydrogen at 6 seconds, placing the carbon–hydrogen backbone of organic chemistry at the two
nodes of the invariant. The Earth is the planet at which the planetary-scale resonance coincides
with the carbon nuclear resonance. This paper advances the astrobiological hypothesis that
abiogenesis requires the resonance between the Earth's planetary-scale invariant and the particle-
scale invariant of the matter on it. The hypothesis predicts that exoplanetary systems satisfying
the full UPL architecture should be more likely to host life than systems that do not, and it
identifies specific tests with JWST, PLATO, Europa Clipper, and JUICE. The Jupiter–Europa
system, independently tested by Sambit Tripathy, gives s in the kinetic-energy form
of the resonance, making Europa a second candidate resonant node and a direct target for the
hypothesis.
1. Introduction
This paper is a work in astrobiology. It asks a specific question: is the origin of life on Earth
connected to a resonance between the planetary scale and the particle scale, and if so, can that
connection be tested with current and near-future space telescopes?
The question is not new. Astrobiology has long asked whether the conditions for life are generic
(life arises wherever liquid water and energy are present) or specific (life requires a particular
planetary architecture, chemistry, or dynamics). The UPL provides a specific form of the
"specific" answer: it says the Earth sits at a resonant node where the planetary-scale invariant and
the particle-scale invariant of carbon coincide, and it predicts that systems without that
coincidence are less likely to host life.
The paper is structured as an astrobiological hypothesis with testable predictions, not as a
derivation of abiogenesis. The derivations of the resonance are in the earlier papers [1–4]. This
paper synthesizes them into an astrobiological claim and identifies the observations that would
test it.

4. The Earth as a resonant node
The Earth satisfies the UPL at the planetary scale: s. Carbon satisfies the sixfold
relation at the nuclear scale: s. The two are within 2% of each other.
The Earth is the planet at which the planetary-scale resonance and the carbon nuclear resonance
coincide. This is a numerical fact about the Earth–Moon–Sun system and the carbon nucleus, not
a claim about the Earth's special status. Other planets do not satisfy the UPL at the one-second
node in the same construction; Jupiter and Saturn, treated as solar-system planets, satisfy a
modified version with the factor replaced by [6] (Appendix 2).
The coincidence is the physical condition under which carbon-based chemistry is stable on a
planet whose dynamics also satisfy the same invariant. It does not guarantee that life will arise. It
does not explain abiogenesis. It explains why, once carbon-based chemistry is present, it is
resonant with the planet it is on.
5. Dynamical questions and the Volynets correction
An earlier draft of the Earth–Moon paper claimed that the Earth–Moon–Sun system sits on a
dynamically stable plateau. An independent analysis by Evgeny Volynets [7] showed that this
claim was incorrect for the reduced isolated model: the resonance function
has a kinematic minimum at km, inside the current lunar orbit. The present system
( ) is past this minimum, not at it.
The revised Appendix 1 of [2] now separates three claims:
1. Empirical observation: s at the present epoch (within 2% of unity).
2. Numerical comparison: the observed rates of lunar recession and terrestrial spin-down are of
the same order as the rates required for , but the tidal/climate decomposition is
uncertain.

6.3 The other Galilean moons
To check whether Europa is a specific hit or part of a distribution, the same formula was applied
to the other Galilean moons and to two other satellite systems:
Orbital Period Comparison!
Europa is the closest match; Callisto is second; the rest give 2–7 s. The formula gives ~1 s for
two systems out of seven. This is not a universal prediction — if it were, all seven would give ~1
s — but it is not obviously chance. A systematic test across all major satellites would distinguish
these.
6.4 Europa as an astrobiological target
Europa is one of the most promising targets for the search for life in the Solar System. Beneath
its icy surface, there is a liquid water ocean of roughly twice the volume of Earth's oceans, kept
liquid by tidal heating from Jupiter's gravity. The ocean is in contact with a rocky mantle, which
could provide the chemical energy and nutrients for life. The scientific case for Europa's
habitability has strengthened since Arthur C. Clarke's 2010: Odyssey Two, in which the monolith
instructs humanity to "attempt no landing there" because life is emerging in the subsurface
ocean.
The Europa Clipper mission (launched October 2024, arriving 2030) and ESA's JUICE mission
(launched 2023, arriving 2031) will characterize Europa's ice shell, ocean, and chemistry.
7. The abiogenesis hypothesis
7.1 The two claims
There are two claims that can be made, and they must be kept distinct.
The weak claim is the boundary-condition argument. The Earth satisfies the UPL at the planetary
scale ( s), carbon sits at the 1-second node of the sixfold relation, and the two are

within 2%. This is a statement about the physical conditions under which carbon-based
chemistry is stable on Earth. It is supported by the UPL's success at both scales.
The strong claim is the abiogenesis hypothesis. It says that abiogenesis — the transition from
non-living chemistry to the first self-replicating system — requires the resonance between the
planetary-scale invariant and the particle-scale invariant. On this hypothesis, the coincidence of
the two scales is not merely a condition under which chemistry is stable; it is a condition without
which abiogenesis cannot occur.
The two claims differ in what they assert. The weak claim says: if carbon-based chemistry is
present on the Earth, it is resonant with the planet. The strong claim says: if a planet does not
satisfy both resonances, carbon-based chemistry will not lead to abiogenesis.
7.2 Why the hypothesis is worth stating
The hypothesis is worth stating because it makes a specific, falsifiable prediction that the
boundary-condition argument does not. If abiogenesis requires the resonance, then:
1. Planets that satisfy the UPL at the planetary scale and contain carbon should be more likely to
host life than planets that satisfy only one of the two.
2. Planets that do not satisfy the UPL at the planetary scale should be less likely to host life, even
if they have the right chemistry.
3. The Earth should be the specific planet at which the coincidence is closest to exact.
The hypothesis can be falsified: if a planet is found that satisfies the planetary resonance but has
no life, that would weaken the strong claim; if a planet is found that does not satisfy the
resonance but has life, that would falsify it directly.
7.3 Why the hypothesis should be stated as a hypothesis
First, the mechanism is not known. The UPL establishes that the resonance holds; it does not
establish that the resonance is a causal factor in abiogenesis. The mechanism by which a
resonance at the planetary scale would influence a chemical reaction at the molecular scale is not
specified.
Second, alternative explanations are not ruled out. The coincidence could be a selection effect
(we observe the resonance because life evolved at the epoch when it holds), a coincidence (the
Earth and carbon happen to be at one second), or a structure. The hypothesis is one of these
alternatives, and it has not been distinguished from the others.
Third, the empirical evidence is not yet decisive. The UPL's success at both scales is evidence
that the resonance is real, but not that it is causally involved in abiogenesis.
of 59 67
7.4 The Noble connection
The hypothesis is a natural extension of Denis Noble's argument about the heartbeat [8]. Noble
argues that the heartbeat's rhythm is not genetically specified because it is a physical property of
the matter the heart is made of. The UPL gives that argument a specific form: the heart beats at
approximately 1 Hz because the particles that constitute cardiac tissue satisfy the one-second
invariant [4].
The abiogenesis hypothesis makes the same move at a larger scale. The chemistry of life is stable
because it is resonant with the planet it is on. The resonance is not imposed from outside; it is a
property of the matter itself. The Noble argument and the abiogenesis hypothesis have the same
structure: biological rhythms and chemical stabilities are not fine-tuned by coincidence; they are
the resonances of the matter.
The difference is that the Noble argument is about the heartbeat, which is a property of an
organism that already exists. The abiogenesis hypothesis is about the origin of the organism. The
Noble argument is supported by the physiology of the heart. The abiogenesis hypothesis is
supported by the UPL's success at both scales, but it is not yet supported by a mechanism.
8. The observational tests
The hypothesis makes specific predictions testable with current and near-future space telescopes.
8.1 JWST transmission spectroscopy
JWST is now capable of detecting biosignature gases — oxygen, ozone, methane, nitrous oxide,
dimethyl sulfide — in the atmospheres of transiting exoplanets. The hypothesis predicts that
among transiting exoplanets with measured atmospheres, those in systems satisfying the UPL
architecture should be more likely to show biosignature combinations than those in systems that
do not. The current sample is small (~10–20 exoplanets with detected atmospheres); the
prediction will become sharper as the sample grows.
8.2 PLATO photometry
The PLATO mission will detect and characterize exoplanets around bright stars, with a specific
focus on habitable-zone rocky planets. PLATO will provide the system architecture — the
presence of asteroid belts, the orbital radii of gas giants, the mass and radius of the habitable-
zone planet — for a large sample. The hypothesis predicts that systems with the full UPL
architecture should be overrepresented among PLATO's habitable-zone detections relative to the
general exoplanet population.
8.3 Exomoon detection
of 60 67
The strongest test of the hypothesis is the detection of exomoons around habitable-zone
exoplanets. The UPL requires a large moon at the resonance. If systems satisfying the UPL
architecture are found to have large moons, and systems without large moons lack biosignatures,
that would be strong support. Exomoon detection is not yet possible with current instruments; it
is a target for the next generation of space telescopes (HabEx, LUVOIR) and for JWST's transit-
timing variations.
8.4 The asteroid belt as a volatile-delivery signature
The UPL predicts an asteroid belt at ~2.4 AU as the volatile-delivery zone. In the Solar System,
the asteroid belt delivered water and organics to the early Earth. If the hypothesis is correct,
systems with a detectable debris belt at ~2.4 AU should be more likely to have habitable-zone
planets with biosignatures. This is testable with ALMA (which can detect debris belts around
nearby stars) and with JWST's mid-infrared observations.
8.5 The Europa Clipper and JUICE tests
If Europa is a second resonant node (§6), the hypothesis predicts that Europa should be habitable
— or at least more likely to be habitable than the other Galilean moons. The Europa Clipper and
JUICE missions will test this in three ways:
1. Ice shell thickness and ocean chemistry. Thin shell and favorable chemistry support
habitability.
2. Plume sampling. If Europa has plumes, the missions could sample the ocean directly.
3. Biosignature detection. Organic molecules or biosignature gases in plumes or the ice shell
would be a direct biosignature.
The hypothesis predicts that Europa should be habitable, not that it should be inhabited. The
missions will test habitability directly and inhabitedness indirectly.
8.6 The statistical test
The hypothesis predicts a statistical correlation between UPL architecture and biosignature
presence. The test is a population-level comparison: among exoplanets with measured
atmospheres and characterized system architecture, the fraction with biosignatures should be
higher for systems satisfying the UPL architecture than for systems that do not. This requires a
sample of 30–50 exoplanets with both atmospheric characterization and system architecture,
which JWST and PLATO together should provide by the late 2020s.
9. What the hypothesis is not
of 61 67
It is not a claim that life must exist wherever the resonance holds. It is a necessary-condition
claim: the resonance is a condition without which abiogenesis is less likely, not a condition that
guarantees it. A planet can satisfy the resonance and still be sterile.
It is not a claim that the Earth is unique. The UPL architecture is a pattern that other systems can
satisfy. The Jupiter–Europa system may be a second example. The KOI-4878 application in the
earlier paper [6] is a first candidate for a star system that may satisfy the architecture.
It is not a replacement for the standard astrobiological criteria (liquid water, energy source,
organic chemistry, sufficient time). It is an additional condition that the standard criteria do not
capture: the resonance between the planetary scale and the particle scale.
It does not claim the sixfold relation extends to bond energies. The bond energies of organic
molecules do not show a sixfold pattern, and this is expected, because the sixfold relation is
about nuclear timescales, not electromagnetic chemistry.
10. Conclusion
The Earth is a resonant node for abiogenesis. This is an astrobiological hypothesis, not a
derivation of life. It is supported by the UPL's success at the particle scale and at the planetary
scale, and it predicts that systems satisfying the UPL architecture should be more likely to host
life than systems that do not.
The prediction is testable with JWST (biosignatures), PLATO (system architecture), ALMA
(debris belts), Europa Clipper and JUICE (Europa's habitability), and future missions
(exomoons). The Jupiter–Europa system is a second candidate resonant node, independently
tested by Tripathy, giving 0.997 s in the kinetic-energy form.
If the prediction holds, it would mean that the conditions for life are not just "liquid water and
energy" but also a specific resonance between the planet and the matter it is made of. If it does
not hold, it would mean that the resonance is a numerical feature of the Solar System but not a
condition for life, which would also be informative.
The hypothesis is offered in the same spirit as Noble's argument about the heartbeat: biological
rhythms and chemical stabilities are not imposed from outside; they are the resonances of the
matter itself.

The Solar System Theory
The idea: We can model the Solar System and the atom such that across these scales, which are
immense, they can be shown as structured according the same physical concepts.
How: To do this we find we can model the Solar System as having a quantum Shrödinger wave
solution, and the atom in terms of its proton, electron, and neutron components as having a
solution as being particles whose inertia is due to their rest motions through time.
The connection: The connection in scales is found to be through a basis unit of one second —
making this unit of time being not just a cultural development handed to us from the ancient
Sumerians when they divided the Earth day into 24 hours, with each hour being 60 minutes, each
minute being 60 seconds — but to be a structural one.
